column2: The second prefatory discussion: on the share of the earth that is settled, with an indication of some of the trees, rivers and zones it contains

Know that it has been shown in the books of the philosophers who study the conditions of the world that the shape of the earth is spherical and that it is surrounded by the element of water, as if it were a grape floating on it. The water drew back from some of its sides because God willed to bring animals into being on it and to have it settled by the human species, which holds the vicegerency over all the rest. From this it may be imagined that the water is beneath the earth, but that is not correct. What is naturally “beneath” is only the heart of the earth, the middle of its sphere, which is its center, which everything seeks by reason of the heaviness in it; and everything other than that, of its sides, [is above]. As for the water that surrounds it, it is above the earth, and if any part of it is said to be beneath the earth, that is only in relation to another side of it. As for the part of the earth from which the water has drawn back, it is half of the surface of its sphere, in the shape of a circle that the watery element surrounds on all its sides as a sea called the Encircling Ocean. It is also called Lablāya, with an emphatic second lām, and it is called Ūqiyānūs — non-Arabic names — and it is called the Green Sea and the Black. Now, of this part of the earth that has been uncovered for settlement, the wastelands and empty land in it are greater than its settlement, and the empty part on the southern side is greater than on the northern side. Only the settled part of it leans toward the northern side, in the shape of a spherical surface that ends on the south at the equator and on the north at a spherical line

and beyond it are the mountains that separate it from the elemental water, and between the two lies the Barrier of Gog and Magog (Yājūj and Mājūj). These mountains incline toward the east, and it ends, in the east and the west, at the element of water as well, in two portions of the encircling circle. They say that this uncovered part of the earth is about half of the sphere or less, and that the settled part of it is about a quarter of it, and this is the part that is divided into the seven zones. The equator divides the earth into two halves from west to east; it is the length of the earth and the greatest line on its sphere, just as the belt of the zodiac and the celestial equator are the greatest line in the heavens. The belt of the zodiac is divided into 360 degrees, and a degree of the earth’s distance is twenty-five farsakhs; the farsakh is 12,000 cubits, the cubit is twenty-four fingers, and the finger is six grains of barley set in a row, stuck together, back to belly. Between the celestial equator, which divides the heavens into two halves and is aligned with the equator on the earth, and each of the two poles there are 90 degrees. But settlement on the northern side of the equator extends 64 degrees, and the remainder of it is empty, with no settlement in it because of the severity of the cold and the freezing, just as the southern side is all empty because of the severity of the heat, all of which we shall show, if God the Exalted wills.

Now those who report on this settled part of the earth and its limits, and on the cities, towns, mountains, seas, rivers, wastelands and sands in it, such as Ptolemy in the book of the Geography and, after him, the author of the Book of Roger (Zakhkhār), divided this settled part into seven divisions, which they call the seven zones, with imaginary limits running between the east and the west, equal in breadth and different in length: the first zone is longer than those after it, and so the second, down to the last, so that the seventh is the shortest, because of what the position of the circle that arose from the drawing back of the water from the sphere of the earth requires. Each of these zones, in their view, is divided into ten sections from west to east in succession, and for each section there is a report on its conditions and the conditions of its settlement. They stated that from the western side of this Encircling Ocean, in the fourth zone, there issues the well-known Mediterranean (the Roman Sea), which begins in a narrow gulf about twelve miles wide, more or less, between Tangier and Tarifa, called the Strait (al-Zuqāq). Then it goes eastward and widens to a breadth of 600 miles, and its end is at the end of the fourth section of the fourth zone, 1,160 farsakhs from its beginning, and there on it are the coasts of Syria. On it from the southern side are the coasts of the Maghrib, the first of which is Tangier at the gulf, then Ifrīqiya, then Barqa as far as Alexandria

and on the northern side are the coasts of Constantinople at the gulf, then the Venetians, then Rome, then the Franks, then al-Andalus as far as Tarifa at the Strait opposite Tangier. This sea is called the Roman Sea and the Syrian Sea, and in it are many large inhabited islands such as Crete, Cyprus, Sicily, Majorca and Sardinia. They said: And from it, on the northern side, two other seas issue, from two gulfs. One of them lies in line with Constantinople; it begins from this sea narrow, the width of a bowshot, and runs through three seas, so that it joins Constantinople; then it widens to a breadth of four miles and runs on in a course of sixty miles, and is called the Gulf of Constantinople. Then it issues from a mouth six miles wide and feeds the Sea of Nīṭish (the Black Sea), a sea that turns from there in its course toward the east, passes the land of Heraclea and ends at the land of the Khazars, 1,300 miles from its mouth, and on both sides of it are nations of the Rūm, the Turks, the Burjān and the Rus. The second of the two seas that issue from the gulfs of this Mediterranean is the Sea of the Venetians; it issues from the land of the Rūm toward the north, and when it reaches the line of the mountain it turns westward to the land of the Venetians and ends at the land of Inkilāya, 1,100 miles from its beginning, and on its two banks are nations of the Venetians, the Rūm and others. It is called the Gulf of the Venetians.

They say that from this Encircling Ocean there also flows, from the east, at 13 degrees north of the equator, a great, wide sea, which runs a little southward until it reaches the first zone, then runs through it westward until it ends, in the fifth section of it, at the lands of Abyssinia and the Zanj and at the land of Bāb al-Mandab, 4,000 farsakhs from its beginning. It is called the Chinese Sea, the Indian Ocean and the Abyssinian Sea. On it, on the southern side, are the land of the Zanj and the land of Barbar, which Imruʾ al-Qays mentioned in his poetry — they are not the Berbers who are the tribes of the Maghrib — then the town of Mogadishu, then the town of Sufāla and the land of Wāqwāq and other nations, beyond whom there is nothing but wastelands and empty land. And on its northern side are China, from its beginning, then India, then Sind, then the coasts of Yemen — from al-Aḥqāf and Zabīd and others — then the land of the Zanj at its end, and after them Abyssinia.

They say that two other seas issue from this Abyssinian Sea. One of them issues from its end at Bāb al-Mandab; it begins narrow, then runs on, widening into a great sea, toward the north and a little to the west, until it ends at al-Qulzum in the fifth section of the second zone, 1,400 miles from its beginning. It is called the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea) and the Sea of Suez, and between it and Fusṭāṭ of Egypt from there are three stages. On it from the east are the coasts of Yemen, then the Hijaz and Jidda, then Madyan, Ayla and Fārān at its end; and from the west the coasts of Upper Egypt, ʿAydhāb, Sawākin and Zaylaʿ, then the land of Abyssinia at its beginning. Its end at al-Qulzum lies in line with the Mediterranean at al-ʿArīsh, with about six stages between them, and kings in Islam and before it have continually sought to cut through what lies between them, but that was never accomplished.

The second sea from this Abyssinian Sea is called the Green Gulf; it issues between the land of Sind and al-Aḥqāf of Yemen and runs toward the north, a little westward, until it ends at al-Ubulla on the coasts of Basra, in the sixth section of the second zone, 440 farsakhs from its beginning. It is called the Persian Gulf (the Sea of Fārs). On it from the east are the coasts of Sind, Makrān, Kirmān, Fārs and al-Ubulla; and at its end, from the west, the coasts of al-Baḥrayn, al-Yamāma, ʿUmān, al-Shiḥr and, at its beginning, al-Aḥqāf. Between the Persian Gulf and al-Qulzum lies the Arabian Peninsula, as though entering from the mainland into the sea: the Abyssinian Sea surrounds it on the south, the Sea of Qulzum on the west and the Persian Gulf on the east, and it opens onto Iraq, between Syria and Basra, with 1,500 miles between the two. There are Kufa, al-Qādisiyya, Baghdad, the Iwān of Kisrā and al-Ḥīra, and beyond that are the non-Arab nations of the Turks, the Khazars and others. In the Arabian Peninsula the lands of the Hijaz are on its western side, the lands of al-Yamāma, al-Baḥrayn and ʿUmān on its eastern side, and the land of Yemen on its southern side, with its coasts on the Abyssinian Sea.

They said: And in this settled part there is another sea, cut off from the other seas, in the north, in the land of Daylam, called the Sea of Jurjān and Ṭabaristān (the Caspian Sea), 1,000 miles long by 600 miles wide. On its west are Azerbaijan and Daylam, on its east the land of the Turks and Khwārazm, on its south Ṭabaristān, and on its north the land of the Khazars and the Alans. This is the sum of the well-known seas that the geographers have mentioned. They said: And in this settled part there are many rivers, the greatest of them four: the Nile, the Euphrates, the Tigris and the river of Balkh called the Jayḥūn. As for the Nile, its source is a great mountain 16 degrees beyond the equator, in line with the fourth section of the first zone, called the Mountain of the Moon; no mountain on earth is known to be higher than it. Many springs issue from it, some of which flow into a lake there and some into another; then rivers issue from the two lakes and all flow into a single lake at the equator, ten stages from the mountain. From this lake two rivers issue. One of them goes toward the north, in line with it, and passes through the land of Nubia, then the land of Egypt; when it has passed beyond it, it divides into closely spaced channels, each of which is called a khalīj (canal)

and all of them flow into the Mediterranean at Alexandria; it is called the Nile of Egypt, and on it Upper Egypt lies on its east and the oases on its west. The other turns off toward the west, then runs along its line until it flows into the Encircling Ocean; it is the river of the Sudan (the land of the black peoples), and all their nations are on its two banks. As for the Euphrates, its source is in the land of Armenia, in the sixth section of the fifth zone, and it runs southward through the land of the Rūm and Malaṭya to Manbij, then passes Ṣiffīn, then al-Raqqa, then Kufa, until it ends at the Baṭḥāʾ, the lowland between Basra and Wāsiṭ, and from there it flows into the Abyssinian Sea. Many rivers are drawn into it on its way, and other rivers issue from it and flow into the Tigris. As for the Tigris, its source is a spring in the land of Khilāṭ, in Armenia as well, and it runs southward past Mosul, Azerbaijan and Baghdad to Wāsiṭ, where it divides into canals, all of which flow into the lake of Basra and reach the Persian Gulf. It lies to the east, on the right of the Euphrates, and many great rivers are drawn into it from every side. Between the Euphrates and the Tigris, from its beginning, lies the Jazīra of Mosul, facing Syria from the two banks of the Euphrates and facing Azerbaijan from the bank of the Tigris.

As for the river Jayḥūn, its source is at Balkh, in the eighth section of the third zone, from many springs there, and great rivers are drawn into it. It runs from south to north and passes through the land of Khurāsān, then leaves it for the land of Khwārazm, in the eighth section of the fifth zone, and flows into the lake of Jurjāniyya, which lies below its city; it is a month’s journey long and as much wide. Into it flows the river of Farghāna and al-Shāsh, which comes from the land of the Turks. On the west of the river Jayḥūn are the lands of Khurāsān and Khwārazm, and on its east the lands of Bukhara, Tirmidh and Samarkand; from there to what lies beyond are the lands of the Turks, Farghāna, al-Khazlajiyya and the non-Arab nations. Ptolemy mentioned all of that in his book, and al-Sharīf in the Book of Roger, and in the Geography they depicted everything in the settled part — mountains, seas and valleys — and covered fully in it what we have no need of, because of its length and because our concern is, for the most part, only with the Maghrib, which is the homeland of the Berbers, and with the homelands that belong to the Arabs in the East; and God is the one who grants success.
A supplement to this second prefatory discussion: that the northern quarter of the earth is more settled than the southern quarter, and the reason for this

We see, from observation and well-attested reports, that the first and second of the settled zones are less settled than those after them; and what settlement there is in them is interspersed with empty land, wastelands, sands, and the Indian Ocean, which lies to the east of the two. The nations of these two zones and their people are not extremely numerous, and their cities and towns are likewise. The third and the fourth and those after them are the opposite: wastelands in them are few, and sands likewise, or absent, and their nations and people exceed all bounds in number, and their cities and towns exceed all bounds in count, and settlement in them is contained between the third and the sixth, while the south is all empty. Many of the philosophers have said that this is because of the excess of heat and the small inclination of the sun in them away from the zenith. So let us make that clear by its proof, from which the reason will become evident for the abundance of settlement between the third and the fourth on the northern side up to the fifth and the seventh. We say: when the two poles of the heavens, the southern and the northern, are on the horizon, there is a great circle there that divides the heavens into two halves; it is the greatest of the circles that pass from east to west, and it is called the celestial equator. It has been shown in its place in astronomy that the uppermost sphere moves from east to west in a daily motion by which it forcibly moves all the other spheres within it, and this motion is perceptible to the senses; and likewise it has been shown that the planets in their spheres have a motion contrary to this one, from west to east, and their durations differ according to the difference in the planets’ motion, in speed and slowness

and the paths of these planets in their spheres are all paralleled by a great circle of the uppermost sphere that divides it into two halves; it is the circle of the zodiac, divided into twelve signs, and it intersects, as has been shown in its place, the celestial equator at two opposite points of the signs, the beginning of Aries and the beginning of Libra, so that the celestial equator divides it into two halves: a half inclined from the celestial equator to the north, which runs from the beginning of Aries to the end of Virgo, and a half inclined from it to the south, which runs from the beginning of Libra to the end of Pisces. When the two poles lie on the horizon in all regions of the earth, there is on the surface of the earth one line, in line with the celestial equator, running from west to east, called the equator. This line fell, by observation, as they claim, at the beginning of the first of the seven zones. All settlement is on the northern side; [the pole] rises above the horizons of this settled part by degrees until its elevation reaches 64 degrees, and there settlement ends, which is the end of the seventh zone. And when it rises above the horizon 90 degrees, which is [the distance] between the pole and the celestial equator on the horizon, six of the signs remain above the horizon, the northern ones, and six below the horizon, the southern ones. And settlement between the four

and sixty up to the ninety is impossible, because heat and cold then do not occur mixed, owing to the length of time between them, so generation (takwīn) does not take place. So the sun is at the zenith at the equator, at the beginning of Aries and Libra, then declines from the zenith toward the beginning of Cancer and the beginning of Capricorn, and the limit of its declination from the celestial equator is 24 degrees. Then, when the north pole rises above the horizon, the celestial equator declines from the zenith by the amount of its elevation, and the south pole sinks likewise by an equal amount in the three, and that is what the timekeepers call the latitude of the place. And when the celestial equator declines from the zenith, the northern signs rise above it, successively, in the amount of their elevation, up to the beginning of Cancer, and the southern signs sink from the horizon likewise, up to the beginning of Capricorn, because of their inclination to the two sides at the equatorial horizon, as we have said. The northern horizon goes on rising until the farthest of the northern [signs], which is the beginning of Cancer, comes to be at the zenith, and that is where the latitude of the place is 24, in the Hijaz and what adjoins it. This is the inclination by which, when the beginning of Cancer declines from the celestial equator at the equatorial horizon, it rises with the elevation of the north pole until it comes to be at the zenith. When the pole rises by more than four

and twenty, the sun descends from the zenith, and goes on descending until the elevation of the pole is 64, and the sun’s descent from the zenith is likewise, and the descent of the south pole below the horizon is the same, so generation ceases because of the excess of cold and frost and its long duration, unmixed with heat. Now the sun, at the zenith and near it, sends its rays upright, and short of the zenith at obtuse and acute angles; and when the angles of the rays are right angles, the light is great and spreads, unlike the case with obtuse and acute angles. For this reason the heat at the zenith and near it is greater than it is farther away, because light is the cause of heat and warming.

Now being at the zenith at the equator occurs twice a year, at the points of Aries and Libra, and when the sun declines, it is not far off, and the heat hardly moderates at the end of its declination, at the beginning of Cancer and Capricorn, before it climbs back to the zenith, so the right-angled rays remain bearing down on that horizon, and their stay is long or continual, so the air is inflamed with heat and its intensity is excessive. Likewise, as long as the sun is at the zenith twice [a year] beyond the equator up to latitude 24, the rays bear down on the horizon there almost as they do at the equator. Excessive heat produces in the air a drying and aridity that prevent generation, because when heat is excessive, waters and moistures dry up and generation in minerals, animals and plants is spoiled, since generation takes place only through moisture. Then, when the beginning of Cancer declines from the zenith at latitude 25 and beyond, the sun descends from the zenith, so the heat comes to moderation or departs from it only slightly; then generation takes place and increases by degrees until the cold becomes excessive in its intensity because of the scarcity of light and the rays being at obtuse angles, so generation diminishes and is spoiled, except that

the spoiling of generation from the intensity of heat is greater than from the intensity of cold, because heat acts more quickly in drying than cold does in freezing. That is why settlement in the first and second zones is slight, in the third, fourth and fifth moderate, because the heat is tempered by the decrease of light, and in the sixth and seventh abundant, because of the decrease of heat, and because the quality of cold, at its beginning, does not affect the spoiling of generation as heat does, since there is no drying in it except at the extreme, through the dryness that then befalls it, as beyond the seventh. For this reason settlement in the northern quarter is greater and more abundant, and God knows best. From this the philosophers took the emptiness of the equator and what lies beyond it, and it was objected against them that it is settled, by observation and well-attested reports; so how can the proof of that be complete? It appears that they did not mean the complete impossibility of settlement in it; rather, the proof led them to hold that the spoiling of generation there is strong through the excess of heat, and that settlement there is either impossible or possible only in the minority of cases. And so it is: for the equator and what lies beyond it, even if there is some settlement there, as is reported, is very slight.

Ibn Rushd has claimed that the equator is temperate and that what lies beyond it in the south is like what lies beyond it in the north, so as much of it is settled as of the latter. What he said is not impossible from the standpoint of the spoiling of generation; it is impossible only in what lies beyond the equator in the south, on the ground that the watery element has covered the face of the earth there up to the limit which, opposite it on the northern side, was receptive of generation. And when the temperate part became impossible because of the water’s concealing it, what lies beyond it followed, since settlement is graded and begins its gradation from the side of existence, not from the side of impossibility. As for the claim that it is impossible at the equator, well-attested transmission refutes it, and God knows best. After this discussion let us draw the picture of the geography as the author of the Book of Roger drew it, and then proceed to discuss it in detail to the end.
A detailed discussion of this geography

Know that the philosophers divided this settled part, as mentioned earlier, into seven divisions from the north to the south, calling each division a zone; so the whole settled part of the earth is divided into these seven zones, each of which extends along its length from the west to the east.

The first of them runs from the west to the east with the equator as its limit on the south, and beyond it there are only wastelands and sands and some settlement which, if it is genuine, is as good as no settlement. Next to it on the north is the second zone, then the third likewise, then the fourth, the fifth, the sixth and the seventh, which is the end of settlement on the northern side. Beyond the seventh there are only empty land and wastelands until it reaches the Encircling Ocean, as is the case beyond the first zone on the south, except that the empty land on the north is much less than the empty land on the south. Then the durations of night and day differ in these zones because of the sun’s declination from the celestial equator and the elevation of the north pole above their horizons, so the arc of night and day differs accordingly; and the length of night and day at the end of the first zone — which is when the sun enters the beginning of Capricorn for the night and the beginning of Cancer for the day — reaches, for each of them, 13 hours. Likewise at the end of the second zone, on the side next to the north, the length of the day there reaches, when the sun enters the beginning of Cancer, which is its summer solstice, 13½ hours, and the same is the longest night at its winter solstice at the beginning of Capricorn, and there remains for the shortest of the night

and the day what remains after the 13½ of the sum of the 24 hours of time for night and day together, which is the complete revolution of the heavens. Likewise at the end of the third zone, on the northern side as well, they reach 14 hours, at the end of the fourth 14½ hours, at the end of the fifth 15 hours, at the end of the sixth 15½, and at the end of the seventh 16 hours, and there settlement ends. So the difference between these zones in the longest of their night and day is half an hour for each zone, increasing from its beginning on the southern side to its end on the northern side, distributed over the parts of this distance. As for the latitude of places in these zones, it is an expression for the distance between the zenith of the place and the celestial equator, which is the zenith of the equator; and by exactly the same amount the south pole sinks below the horizon of that place and the north pole rises above it; these are three equal distances, called the latitude of the place, as was mentioned before.

Those who discuss this geography divided each of these seven zones along its length, from west to east, into ten equal sections, and they mention what each section contains of lands, cities, mountains, rivers, and the distances between them along the routes. We shall now give a brief account of that and mention the famous lands, rivers and seas in each section of them, following in that what occurs in the Nuzhat al-mushtāq (“The Delight of One Who Longs”), which the ʿAlid Idrisid Ḥammūdid wrote for the king of Sicily from among the Franks, who is Roger son of Roger (Zakhkhār ibn Zakhkhār), when he was staying with him in Sicily after Sicily’s leaving the emirate of Malaga. He wrote the book in the middle of the sixth century, and collected for him many books by al-Masʿūdī, Ibn Khurradādhbih, al-Ḥawqalī, al-Qadarī, Ibn Isḥāq the astronomer, Ptolemy and others. We begin with the first zone and go on to the last, and God, glory be to Him, the Exalted, guards us by His favor and grace.
The first zone,

In it, on its western side, are the Fortunate Islands (al-Jazāʾir al-Khālidāt), from which Ptolemy began taking the longitudes of the lands; they are not in the expanse of the zone but are islands in the Encircling Ocean, many in number, the largest and most famous being three, and it is said that they are inhabited. It has reached us that ships of the Franks passed by them in the middle of this century and fought them, and took booty from them and took captives, and sold some of their prisoners on the coasts of the Far Maghrib, and these entered the service of the sultan; when they had learned the Arabic language they reported on the condition of their islands: that they dig the ground for planting with horns, that iron is lacking in their land, that their food is barley and their livestock goats, that their fighting is with stones that they throw backward, and their worship is prostration to the sun when it rises, and they know no religion, and no call has reached them. The place of these islands is found only by stumbling upon them, not by aiming at them, because the voyaging of ships on the sea is only by the winds and by knowing the directions from which they blow and to which of the lands that lie in the path of that wind it leads a ship if it passes straight. If the wind varies and it is known where it leads in a straight line, the sail is set to it, aligned so as to carry the ship by it, according to rules for this that are well established among the sailors and mariners, who are the captains of ships at sea. The lands on the shores of the Mediterranean and on its other bank are all written on a sheet in the form they have in reality

and in their placement on the coasts of the sea in their order, and the places the winds blow from and their paths, in their variations, [are written] along with them on that sheet. They call it the compass chart (al-kunbāṣ), and on it they rely in their voyages. All of this is lacking in the Encircling Ocean, which is why ships do not enter it, because if they disappear from sight of the coasts, they will rarely find their way back to them, in addition to the vapors that form in the air of this sea and on the surface of its water and hinder ships in their course; because of their distance, the rays of the sun reflected from the surface of the earth do not reach them to dissolve them. Therefore finding the way to them is hard and getting news of them is difficult. As for the first section of this zone, in it is the mouth of the Nile that comes from its source at the Mountain of the Moon, as we mentioned; it is called the Nile of the Sudan, and it goes to the Encircling Ocean and flows into it at the island of Awlīk. On this Nile are the city of Salā, Takrūr and Ghāna, all of which at the present time are within the kingdom of the king of Mālī, of the nations of the Sudan; to their lands the merchants of the Far Maghrib travel. Near them, to their north, are the land of Lamtūna and all the other groups of the Veiled People (al-Mulaththamūn), and desert tracts in which they roam. South of this Nile is a people of the Sudan called “Lamlam”; they are unbelievers, and they brand their faces and temples. The people of Ghāna and Takrūr raid them, take them captive, and sell them to the merchants

and they bring them to the Maghrib; and all of them, for the most part, are their slaves. Beyond them in the south there is no settlement worth considering, only people closer to speechless animals than to rational beings, who live in the wilds and caves and eat herbage and grains unprepared, and sometimes eat one another; they are not counted among human beings. The fruits of the lands of the Sudan all come from the fortified villages of the desert of the Maghrib, such as Tuwāt, Tikdarārīn and Wargalān. In Ghāna there was, it is said, a kingship and a dynasty of a people of the ʿAlids known as the Banū Ṣāliḥ; the author of the Book of Roger said that he is Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan, but this Ṣāliḥ is not known among the descendants of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥasan. This dynasty has gone at the present time, and Ghāna has come to belong to the sultan of Mālī. East of this country, in the third section of the zone, is the town of (Kūkū), on a river that rises from some mountains there and flows westward and sinks into the sands of the second section. The kingship of Kūkū stood on its own, then the sultan of Mālī took it over and it became part of his kingdom, and it has fallen into ruin at the present time on account of a civil strife

that took place there, which we shall mention when we come to the dynasty of Mālī, in its place in the history of the Berbers. South of the town of Kūkū is the land of Kātam, of the nations of the Sudan, and after them Wangāra, on the bank of the Nile on its northern side; and east of the lands of Wangāra and Kātam are the lands of Zaghāwa and Tājira, adjoining the land of Nubia, in the fourth section of this zone. In it passes the Nile of Egypt, going from its source at the equator to the Mediterranean in the north. The source of this Nile is the Mountain of the Moon, which lies 16 degrees beyond the equator. They differ over the vocalization of this word: some vocalize it with a fatḥa on the qāf and the mīm (Qamar), after the moon of the sky, for its intense whiteness and abundant light; and in the book al-Mushtarak (“The Homonyms”) by Yāqūt it has a ḍamma on the qāf and a sukūn on the mīm (Qumr), after a group of the people of India; and Ibn Saʿīd likewise vocalized it so. Ten springs issue from this mountain, each five of which gather in a lake, with six miles between the two; and from each of the two lakes three rivers issue, which all gather in a single marsh, at the lower end of which a mountain lies across and splits the lake from the north side, and its water is divided into two parts. The western part runs to the lands of the Sudan westward until it flows into the Encircling Ocean, and the eastern part issues going to the north, past the lands of Abyssinia and Nubia and what lies between them, and divides in the upper part of the land of Egypt

and three of its channels flow into the Mediterranean at Alexandria, Rosetta and Damietta, and one flows into a salt lake before it joins the sea, in the middle of this first zone. On this Nile are the lands of Nubia and Abyssinia and some of the land of the oases as far as Aswān. The capital of the land of Nubia is the city of Dongola, which is on the west of this Nile; after it come ʿAlwa and Bilāq, and after them the Mountain of the Cataracts, six stages north of Bilāq. It is a mountain high on the side of Egypt and low on the side of Nubia, and the Nile passes through it and pours into a deep chasm in a terrifying torrent, so that ships cannot pass through it; rather, the cargo of the ships of the Sudan is transferred and carried on the back to the town of Aswān, the capital of Upper Egypt, up to above the cataracts. Between the cataracts and Aswān are twelve stages, and the oases are to the west of it, on the bank of the Nile, and are now in ruins, with traces of ancient settlement in them. In the middle of this zone, in the fifth section of it, is the land of Abyssinia, on a valley that comes from beyond the equator, going to the land of Nubia, where it flows into the Nile descending to Egypt. Many people have been mistaken about it and have claimed that it is of the Nile of the Moon, but Ptolemy mentioned it in the Geography and stated that it is not of this Nile.

To the middle of this zone, in the fifth section, the Indian Ocean ends, which enters from the side of China and covers most of this zone up to this fifth section, so no settlement remains in it except what is on the islands within it — they are many, said to number 1,000 islands — or on its coasts on the northern side; and of these in this first zone there is only a corner of the land of China on the east, and in the land of Yemen. In the sixth section of this zone, between the two seas that descend from this Indian Ocean toward the north, namely the Sea of Qulzum and the Persian Gulf — and between them lies the Arabian Peninsula, which comprises the lands of Yemen and al-Shiḥr in its east, on the coast of this Indian Ocean, and the lands of the Hijaz, al-Yamāma and what adjoins them, as we shall mention in the second zone and those after it — as for what is on the coast of this sea on its west, it is the town of Zālaʿ, on the edges of the land of Abyssinia, and the territories of the Bujā in the north of Abyssinia, between Jabal al-ʿAlāqī in the upper reaches of Upper Egypt and the Sea of Qulzum that descends from the Indian Ocean

and below the land of Zālaʿ on the north side in this section is the Gulf of Bāb al-Mandab, where the sea that descends there narrows through the pressure of the Mountain of al-Mandab, which leans into the middle of the Indian Ocean, extending along the coast of Yemen from south to north for twelve miles, so that because of this the sea narrows until its breadth becomes three miles or so; it is called Bāb al-Mandab. On it the ships of Yemen pass to the coast of Suez, near Egypt. Below Bāb al-Mandab are the island of Sawākin and Dahlak; and facing it on its west are the territories of the Bujā, of the nations of the Sudan, as we mentioned; and on its east in this section are the Tihāmas of Yemen, among which on its coast is the town of ʿAlī ibn Yaʿqūb. To the south of the town of Zālaʿ, on the coast of this sea on its west, are the villages of Barbar, one after another, and it [the coast] curves from its south to the end of the sixth section; and next to them there, on their east, is the land of the Zanj, then the land of Sufāla; on its southern coast is the land of Wāqwāq, continuing to the end of the tenth section of this zone at the entrance of this sea from the Encircling Ocean. As for the islands of this sea, they are many.

Among the greatest of them is the island of Sarandīb, round in shape. In it is the famous mountain, of which it is said that there is none higher on earth, and it lies opposite Sufāla. Then the island of al-Qamar, an elongated island that begins opposite the land of Sufāla and goes toward the east, deviating greatly, until it comes close to the coasts of upper China; around it in this sea are, on its south, the islands of Wāqwāq, and on its east, the islands of al-Sīlān, besides other islands in this sea, great in number, in which are kinds of perfumes and spices and in which, it is said, are mines of gold and emerald; most of their people follow the religion of the Magians, and they have many kings; and in these islands, as to the conditions of settlement, are wonders that the geographers have mentioned. On the northern side of this sea, in the sixth section of this zone, are the lands of Yemen, all of them: on the side of the Sea of Qulzum the town of Zabīd and al-Mahjam and the Tihāma of Yemen, and after them the town of Ṣaʿda, the seat of the Zaydī imamate, which is far from the southern sea and from the eastern sea; and beyond that the city of Aden, north of which is Sanaa; and after them, toward the east, the land of al-Aḥqāf and Ẓafār, and after them the land of Hadramawt, then the land of al-Shiḥr, between the southern sea and the Persian Gulf.
